analysis.one_liner: Forces pharmacy benefit managers to disclose drug pricing and rebates and treat pharmacies fairly.
analysis.headline: The bill won 34 bipartisan cosponsors but never received a committee vote or a House floor vote before Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) — the middlemen that insurers and employers hire to run prescription drug coverage — to report each year to plan sponsors on what they pay pharmacies, what they collect from drug makers, and how often they steer patients to pricier drugs or their own pharmacies. It would also have required PBMs to pay pharmacies promptly, share their pricing formulas, limit aggressive audits of pharmacies, and get permission before selling patient claims data. The House referred it to three committees, where it received no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with prescription drug coverage, employers and unions that sponsor health plans, and community pharmacies. Plan sponsors would finally see the rebates and fees PBMs collect and whether PBMs switch patients to higher-cost drugs; pharmacies would get faster payment, transparent pricing updates, and protection from retroactive audit clawbacks and from being steered into PBMs' own mail-order pharmacies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured consumers, employers, and local pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: PBMs would have to report annually to each plan sponsor on prescription counts and costs, payments to pharmacies, and all rebates, discounts, and other payments from pharmaceutical manufacturers, including how much was shared with the plan.

The bill would prohibit PBMs from mandating use of, or giving incentives for, a pharmacy the PBM owns, and would bar PBMs from moving patients off a lower-cost drug to a higher-cost one without explaining the change to the plan sponsor.
PBMs would have to publish and update their Maximum Allowable Cost pricing lists, pay pharmacies promptly for clean claims, and could not exclude qualified pharmacies willing to accept their terms.

PBM audits of pharmacies would be limited to two years of records, could not use statistical extrapolation to calculate clawbacks, and could not recoup clerical errors unless fraud or actual harm was shown.
PBMs would need written plan-sponsor approval and a 30-day notice before selling or leasing patient utilization or claims data, and individuals could opt out of the sale of their data.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers, who would lose the opacity that hides their rebates, spreads, audit clawbacks, and ownership conflicts from the plans and patients they serve. Insurers and plan sponsors would face modest oversight costs passed through premiums.

drawbacks.text: Annual disclosure and pricing-update requirements add administrative work for PBMs and insurers, and some of that cost could be passed on to plan sponsors and premiums.

Limiting audits to two years and barring statistical extrapolation, while protecting pharmacies from arbitrary clawbacks, would also make it somewhat easier for pharmacy billing fraud to go undetected.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed real, documented conflicts of interest in drug benefit management — hidden rebates, self-dealing toward PBM-owned pharmacies, and aggressive audit recoupments — with disclosure and fair-dealing rules rather than price controls. The administrative costs are modest next to the visibility it would have given employers, unions, and Medicare into how their drug money is spent, and the audit limits include a fraud exception, though they lean toward pharmacy protection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and subcommittees in 2011, never received a markup or vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers introduced the bill on May 24, 2011, joined by Rep. Anthony Weiner as co-lead.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce committees, and in June and September 2011 to subcommittees in each.
The bill drew 34 cosponsors, 24 Democrats and 10 Republicans.
No committee reported the bill and the House never voted on it; no further action is recorded after September 8, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers were better off: the 112th Congress ended with no federal requirement that they disclose rebates and fees, pay pharmacies promptly, or disclose their ownership conflicts, and no successor version of this bill moved either.

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines from the start: a Republican lead sponsor and a Democratic co-lead, with 24 of the 34 cosponsors being Democrats and 10 Republicans.

industries.note: The bill targeted PBMs directly: they would have had to disclose rebates and spreads, pay pharmacies promptly, share pricing formulas, limit audit clawbacks, and stop steering patients to pharmacies they own. Their business depends on the opacity and conflicts this bill would have removed.

Pharmacies would get transparent and weekly-updated reimbursement pricing, prompt payment for clean claims, protection from statistical-extrapolation audit clawbacks, and freedom from being excluded or forced to buy into PBM-owned mail-order operations.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors
industries.note: Insurers, employers, and unions that hire PBMs would receive annual reports on prescription costs, manufacturer rebates, generic dispensing rates, and drug-switching driven by PBM policies — information that would let them negotiate harder on behalf of plan members.

The bill would not regulate manufacturers directly, but the required disclosure of all rebates, discounts, and other payments to PBMs would expose the price-concession deals that keep list prices and net prices far apart.
